newsitem.title: Iran: Iran prepares for election after fierce campaign.
newsitem.headline: Iran prepares for election after fierce campaign.

text.p: Iranians prepared to vote for a new president as authorities promised voters that Friday's election would be fair despite rumours of possible vote-rigging.

Hundreds of youths were out on the streets through Wednesday night, waving posters of former cabinet minister Mohammad Khatami, a leading candidate, at passing motorists as 12 days of heated campaigning came to an end on Thursday.

"I've been out all night pasting up posters," said Javad, a university student in Khatami's army of young volunteers who have waged a nightly poster war with supporters of his main rival, conservative Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.

Posters of Nateq-Nouri were also pasted on walls throughout Tehran but his supporters did not seem to be as active as those of Khatami. Two other candidates are also standing, but they are rated outsiders and given little chance of making an impact.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani rejected any possibility of fraud in the fiercely contested poll to elect his successor.
"The people can be sure that their vote will be the same as the ballot that they wrote and put in the boxes," Rafsanjani told Tehran radio after a visit to the Interior Ministry.

His remarks were the latest assurance by authorities in the face of rumours that officials supporting Nateq-Nouri, who has the backing of key clerical groups, might use their power to influence the vote counting in his favour.
Security forces patrolled key installations in the capital and police moved many of the campaigners on. Some major thoroughfares and intersections were littered with election debris.
The Interior Ministry said 200,000 police were mobilised to provide security for 33,400 voting places which would be set up in mosques, schools and clinics.

Election officials warned against any campaigning past the 8 a.m. (0330 GMT) legal deadline on Thursday and called on some 33 million Iranians 15 years and older to vote as their national and religious duty.
Rafsanjani is obliged by law to step down in August after serving two consecutive four-year terms.
The presidency is Iran's highest elective office but ranks second to that of supreme spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei who has absolute power over all state institutions.
If no clear winner emerges with more than 50 percent of the votes a run-off will be held between the two candidates getting the most votes.
The four candidates were permitted to stand from among 238 hopefuls who were screened for their belief in Iran's Islamic system of government.
Iranian analysts and Western diplomats said the election was too close to call. The few opinion polls during the campaign have showed no common trend in voting intentions.
A high turnout is expected after the liveliest election campaign since Shi'ite Moslem clerics led a revolution that toppled the Shah in 1979.
"This election has turned into a referendum on the mullahs," a Western diplomat said. "For the first time since the revolution there is a real debate going on.
"Many people say they will vote for Khatami but they expect Nateq-Nouri to become president."

While both of the two leading candidates are 54-year-old Shi'ite clergymen, Khatami is seen as having more liberal views and standing for a looser interpretation of the Islamic norms of behaviour enforced since the revolution. He is popular among women, students and intellectuals.

Nateq-Nouri holds conservative Islamic views and is backed by Iran's traditional merchant class of bazaaris. Wide segments of the clerical establishment stepped up their efforts in Nateq-Nouri's favour after sympathetic remarks by Khamenei, who stopped short of openly backing him.

Some 280 people were arrested in Tehran up to Sunday for unspecified election violations. No further arrests have been announced, but Khatami's election headquarters was shut down on Wednesday for alleged violations of election laws.
